hook: Mr. Okafor, 72, has been vomiting for two days and can barely stand. His nurse hangs a bag labeled "0.9% sodium chloride" and explains that its dissolved particles are close to those of his own blood. What does 0.9% mean, why does the particle count matter, and what makes sodium chloride dissolve at all? The answers all start with the water molecule.

prereq.q: Why is a water molecule polar?
options: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder than hydrogen, and the molecule is bent
Oxygen and hydrogen share electrons exactly equally
Water is held together by ionic bonds
prereq.why: Unequal sharing leaves oxygen partly negative and the hydrogens partly positive, and the bent shape keeps those partial charges from canceling.

options: A shared pair of electrons between hydrogen and oxygen in one molecule
A weak attraction between a partly positive hydrogen and a partly negative oxygen or nitrogen nearby
The transfer of an electron from hydrogen to another atom
prereq.why: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between partial charges, usually between neighboring molecules. No electrons are shared or transferred.

prereq.q: What happens to an ionic compound such as potassium chloride in water?
options: It stays as whole units held by covalent bonds
Its ions separate and spread through the water
Its ions gain protons and become neutral
prereq.why: Ionic bonds are weak in water. The ions separate and become free electrolytes.

anatomy.caption: Water dissolving sodium chloride. Oxygen ends of water molecules surround each sodium ion; hydrogen ends surround each chloride ion.

chain.cause: Water's oxygen end is partly negative and its hydrogen ends are partly positive.
chain.effect: Water molecules are attracted to ions: oxygen ends turn toward Na+ and hydrogen ends toward Cl−.

chain.cause: Many water molecules pull on each ion at the surface of a sodium chloride crystal.
chain.effect: The ions are pulled out one by one, and each travels wrapped in a shell of water.

chain.cause: The freed ions spread evenly through the water.
chain.effect: A solution forms, and its concentration is the amount of sodium chloride divided by the volume: 9 g in a liter is 154 mmol/L.

chain.cause: Each unit of sodium chloride releases two particles, Na+ and Cl−.
chain.effect: The solution's osmolarity, its total count of dissolved particles, is about twice its sodium chloride concentration: 154 × 2 ≈ 308 mOsm/L.

chain.cause: Body fluid then loses water while keeping its dissolved particles, as when someone drinks nothing for days.
chain.effect: The same particles sit in less water, so sodium concentration and osmolality both rise.

ideas: Hydrogen bonds pull your water molecules toward each other, a property called cohesion. Molecules at the surface have water neighbors only below and beside them, so they are pulled inward and the surface acts like a stretched skin. This inward pull is surface tension.

A solution is a mixture in which one substance is spread evenly, particle by particle, through another. The solute (solutus = loosened) is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent (solvere = to loosen) is what it dissolves in. In your body the solvent is almost always water.

A mixture holds substances combined without bonds. A solution's particles are single ions and small molecules that never settle. A colloid (kolla = glue, -oid = like) holds larger particles, such as the very large molecules in your blood's liquid part, that jostling water molecules keep from settling. In a suspension (suspendere = to hang) particles settle once stirring stops, as blood cells sink in a standing tube.

Hydrophilic (hydro- = water, -philic = loving) substances are ions and polar molecules, and they dissolve in water. Hydrophobic (-phobic = fearing) substances are nonpolar, such as oils, and they clump together. Nothing repels them: water molecules hold on to each other by hydrogen bonds and squeeze nonpolar molecules into clusters.

misconception.wrong: A high blood sodium means the body holds too much sodium.
misconception.right: Concentration is amount divided by volume. A person who loses water but not sodium, for example by drinking nothing for days, ends up with a high sodium concentration while holding a normal amount of sodium. A lab value tells you the ratio; the history tells you whether the solute rose or the water fell.

summary: Water is polar and its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other. That gives it a high capacity for heat, cooling as it evaporates, cohesion and surface tension, and the power to dissolve ions and polar molecules. In a solution, the solute dissolves in the solvent. Hydrophilic substances (ions and polar molecules) dissolve; hydrophobic, nonpolar ones are pushed into clusters by water holding on to itself. Mixtures can be solutions, colloids or suspensions, and blood is all three. Concentration is amount of solute divided by volume, measured in percent, mg/dL or mmol/L; it rises when solute is added or water is lost. Osmolarity counts every dissolved particle, each ion separately, and normal blood osmolality is about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg.
